opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because the whole value of something like a time-horizon measurement depends on it telling you something beyond the specific tasks we happened to build.

I think the first thing I'd want is for the held-out set to be constructed by a different process than the original suite. If the same people, with the same instincts about what makes a "good" task, build both sets, then you'll get generalization almost by construction, and it won't tell you much. So I'd want something like: sample tasks from the actual work people do. Take real tickets from software teams, real research requests, real ops work, and then do the minimum amount of processing needed to make them runnable and scorable. The point is to let the distribution be messy in the way real work is messy.

Second, I'd deliberately vary the properties we suspect our benchmark is quietly selecting for. Our tasks tend to be automatically scorable, relatively well-specified, self-contained, and they don't require much interaction with other people or long-lived context. Those are exactly the dimensions where I'd expect generalization to break. So I'd want held-out tasks that are underspecified, where you have to figure out what's actually being asked, tasks that require working inside a large existing codebase with a lot of implicit conventions, tasks where feedback is delayed or noisy. Then you can ask not just "does it generalize?" but "along which axes does it stop generalizing?", which is much more useful.

Third, you need human baselines on the held-out set done the same way, because the time-horizon metric is anchored to how long it takes skilled humans. If the baselining procedure differs, you can't tell whether a discrepancy is about the models or about the measurement.

And then the actual test is something like: fit the logistic curve of success against human time on the original suite, use it to predict success rates on the held-out tasks given their human completion times, and look at calibration. Are we systematically over-predicting? Is the slope different? If the model's fifty-percent horizon on messy real-world tasks is, say, a factor of several shorter than on the benchmark, that's really important to know, and it's plausible that's roughly what you'd find. We've seen hints in that direction when we've looked at messiness scores.

One thing I'd caution about is contamination over time. Once a held-out set gets used and published, it stops being held out. So I'd want a rolling process where you keep collecting fresh tasks, and ideally keep some fraction private.

Honestly, the biggest practical bottleneck is cost. Human baselining of multi-hour tasks is expensive, and getting realistic tasks from organizations runs into confidentiality issues. But I think it's worth it, because otherwise you risk a lot of people reading a trend line as a statement about the world when it might partly be a statement about our task construction process.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a held-out set built through a different process and deliberately varied along dimensions where the benchmark may be selective, including realism, ambiguity, codebase complexity, and feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the thing we're really trying to measure isn't "how good are models at our specific tasks," it's "how good are models at doing real work that matters." And the time horizon result is only interesting insofar as it tracks something real.

So if I were designing a held-out set, the first thing I'd want is for the task distribution to be chosen by different people, with a different process, for different reasons. A lot of the risk with our current suite is that the same handful of people decided what counts as a task, what's in scope, how it gets scored. So you want tasks that were built without knowledge of what's in the main benchmark, and ideally built by people who don't have our priors about what agents are good or bad at. Maybe that's engineers at a few companies who just write down things they actually had to do last month and how long they took, and we never see the task contents until we run them.

Second, I'd want to vary the dimensions we suspect we're overfitting on. Our tasks tend to be pretty clean. They have a clear success criterion, they're self-contained, they run in a sandbox, and we built them so that automatic scoring is possible. Real work is messy. So the held-out set should deliberately include tasks where the spec is underspecified and you have to make a judgment call, tasks that span multiple sessions where you have to pick up context later, tasks that require interacting with a real codebase that has history and conventions, tasks where the "right" answer involves pushing back on the request. Those are all places where I'd expect the horizon to look shorter than our headline number, and I'd want to know by how much.

Third, and this is the one people underrate, you want the human baselines to be collected the same way. A lot of the apparent generalization gap between benchmarks is actually a gap in how the human time estimates were produced. If one set measures expert time with a clock and another relies on self-reports, you'll see differences that have nothing to do with the model. So whatever the held-out set is, I'd insist on paying people to actually do the tasks under comparable conditions.

And then the actual test is simple. You fit the horizon curve on our suite, you predict success rates on the held-out tasks as a function of their human time, and you look at the residuals. If the model's fifty percent horizon on our set is, say, four hours, and on the held-out set it's forty minutes, that's an enormous finding and it tells you the headline number is about our tasks, not about the world. If it's three hours, I'd actually be fairly reassured. My honest guess is it lands somewhere in between, and the interesting part is which task features predict the drop.

The last thing I'd add is you shouldn't do this once. You want to keep generating new held-out tasks over time, because the moment a held-out set exists and people know about it, it starts leaking into training in various ways, and you're back where you started.

r001.rationale: Recommends a held-out set created independently of the benchmark and deliberately varying task features such as ambiguity, multi-session work, real codebases, and judgment calls.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what kind of generalization we care about. If you sample more tasks using the same process that produced the benchmark, you can test whether performance generalizes to new tasks from that distribution. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it generalizes to the work people actually want to delegate to these systems.

For that, I’d want an independently collected set of tasks drawn from some reasonably well-defined population of real work. Ideally, you’d choose the sampling procedure before looking at which tasks the models do well on, and keep the tasks out of the loop for developing the agent as well as the model. You’d also want to avoid selecting only tasks that are easy to turn into automatically graded benchmark problems, because that selection could itself explain a lot of the apparent generalization.

Then I’d use performance on the existing benchmark to make predictions about the held-out set. If the claim is about task length, for example, you’d get independent measurements of how long those tasks take humans and ask whether the relationship between human completion time and model success carries over. I’d look at calibration and at differences across task types, rather than just whether the models have the same ranking.

And I’d probably have several levels of holdout: new tasks in familiar categories, new categories, and tasks collected through a different process altogether. Those test progressively stronger claims. If you only do the first, I think you should be fairly cautious about interpreting the result as evidence for the third.

r001.rationale: The response recommends independently collected held-out tasks from real work, including new categories and tasks gathered through a different process, to test generalization beyond METR's benchmark tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what distribution we want to generalize to. If you take tasks that were collected in the same way as the existing benchmark and randomly hold some out, that’s useful, but it mostly tests generalization within that task collection process. It doesn’t necessarily tell you how well the results transfer to a different kind of work.

So I’d want an independently collected set of tasks, ideally from people doing real work, where the people selecting them aren’t trying to reproduce the benchmark. You could hold out entire task sources or categories, rather than just individual tasks. And you’d want to keep those tasks private and avoid using the results to repeatedly tune the agent, because then they stop being a useful held-out test.

Then I’d make the prediction concrete: given a model’s performance on METR’s benchmark, what do we predict about its performance on this new set? You’d want comparable human baselines and success criteria, so that differences in task difficulty don’t get confused with failures to generalize. And I’d look at both the overall prediction and where it breaks down. Does it transfer across domains? Does it transfer to tasks with more ambiguous instructions or different tools? That would tell us much more than just whether the scores on two benchmarks are correlated.

r001.rationale: It recommends an independently collected held-out set from different task sources or categories, explaining that randomly holding out tasks from the same collection process mainly tests within-process generalization.
